what_this_measures: Whether the camera's up vector is determined by the scan or by the run. The pipeline infers it from the largest planar segment, segment_plane is RANSAC, and the published fields -- source, inlier fraction, tilt -- take overlapping values on both branches when two planes compete, so one run's record cannot show that the next run would roll the view by ninety degrees.
why_it_matters: The up vector is consumed by the view cameras, not merely recorded. An axis chosen by a coin flip is a view rolled onto its side in some fraction of runs, which is the reviewability problem the inference was added to fix.

cases.what_this_cloud_is: A 4x4 floor and a 4x4 wall with 8100 points each. Equal in the quantity segment_plane scores, so the only question is which plane a given fit lands on. This is the failure the repeats exist to catch.

Planes at x=0 and y=0 with 8100 points each. Ambiguous like the room above, but with the declared default reachable by neither branch, so the fallback publishing the default is distinguishable from it publishing whichever branch won.
The same room with a quarter as many wall points. A positive control: the scan does determine an axis and the pipeline must still name it.
And with a tenth, so that 'determined' is not a single example either.
Open3D's own demo capture, the data every accepted record in this directory is built from. The negative control: a measure that fired here would be unusable.

A model with no floor and no wall. The case the repeats do not catch: they agree unanimously on a plane tilted well off the axis it gets snapped to, because one plane does dominate a convex-ish shape.

detection_by_repeat_count.why_it_is_not_one: The check fires when the repeats disagree, so it misses when every fit lands on the same branch. The chance-agreement account of the residual, (1-p)^n + p^n for a per-fit minority rate p over n fits, is consistent with the measurement when the measurement has the power to test it: see does_the_minority_rate_vary_between_processes, which puts 3600 checks against each process's own p and finds the predicted and observed miss counts within a couple of sigma. It is admissible, not confirmed -- the independence it assumes between fits in one run is untested. The rates above are measurements either way and are not derived from any model.

independence_of_the_fits.model_tested: (1-p)^n + p^n, for n fits and a fixed per-fit minority p
independence_of_the_fits.exponent_is: the number of fits, which is one plus the repeats
independence_of_the_fits.this_verdict_does_not_reproduce: and that is the point -- see across_processes below. One process is not enough to decide this, so no verdict is published from this block alone

and_does_it_predict_the_miss_rate.so: stated as the comparison rather than as a verdict, because the quantity that decides it is a gap in sigmas and a reader should see both terms

the_sign_of_this_gap_is_not_a_finding.what_the_first_two_looked_like: a systematic over-prediction of about 12 percent, which would mean the fits are not quite independent and the check misses slightly less often than chance alone would make it
the_sign_of_this_gap_is_not_a_finding.what_happened_next: the third run came back at +0.13 and the apparent bias was gone. Draws spanning a couple of sigma are unremarkable for a quantity whose unit is one sigma, and the gap published above is a further independent draw a reader can add to the list
the_sign_of_this_gap_is_not_a_finding.retained_because: the response to those first two readings was to double the checks per process so a 12 percent bias would clear three sigma. That is the defect this whole record is about -- reading a figure that has not been shown to reproduce -- and it was about to be committed by the author of the record. Running the block again cost four minutes and was the only thing that caught it

does_the_minority_rate_vary_between_proc.so: at ten times the power the four-process probe had, the per-process minority rates are consistent with one fixed rate: the chi-square per degree of freedom is near one and the spread is a couple of sigma of counting noise, where a rate genuinely spanning 0.2 to 0.375 would now be eight. The variation the low-power probe saw was its own noise. This removes the reason that probe gave for withdrawing the chance-agreement model, so a fixed-p model is admissible on this evidence
does_the_minority_rate_vary_between_proc.what_this_still_does_not_establish: that the model is correct. Admissible is not confirmed: this measures the rate's stability across processes, not whether the fits within one pipeline run are independent of each other, which is the assumption the model actually needs. The detection rates published above do not depend on it either way
does_the_minority_rate_vary_between_proc.this_supersedes: `repeats_within_one_process` below, which is retained because its spread is what prompted this one. Two things were wrong with it and both are recorded rather than quietly fixed: it was named for separate processes and used none, so its spread was never the between-process quantity it was built to test; and at forty fits it could not have decided either way. It was right to call its own result undecidable

repeats_within_one_process.so: nothing, on its own. At forty fits per estimate this probe could not separate a varying rate from counting noise in either direction, and it was measuring repeated runs in one process while reporting them as separate processes. Its verdicts are retained as observations. The between-process question it was built for is answered at ten times this power by `does_the_minority_rate_vary_between_processes` above
repeats_within_one_process.what_would_settle_it: a few hundred fits per process across a dozen processes would separate a varying rate from counting noise. That is a question about RANSAC's threading, not about whether this check works, so it is named rather than answered here

independence_of_the_fits.what_this_does_not_change: the check still detects the ambiguity in most runs at the shipped count, and the rate is published rather than claimed away. Nothing above is derived from the chance-agreement account, so whether that account holds changes the explanation of why the check misses and not the measurement of how often

what_the_cases_establish: A single fit on the ambiguous room returns two different axes, and the inlier fraction and tilt ranges of the two branches overlap, so no field the function publishes separates them.
Seeding does not settle it: ten fits with the same seed re-set before each one return both axes.
With the repeats, the ambiguous room publishes the declared default labelled as the default in most runs, instead of one of the two branches labelled as measured in every run.
All three determined clouds -- two constructed, one real -- still get a named axis, so the check does not refuse to answer on data that has an answer.
what_this_does_not_claim: Not that the check always fires: detection_by_repeat_count gives its measured rate at three repeat counts, and the misses are accounted for by the branches agreeing by chance. Not that repeat agreement means the axis is right -- the armadillo case agrees unanimously on a plane tilted 19 degrees off the axis it is snapped to, holding 13% of the points, just above the one-tenth floor the weak-plane guard enforces. And not a calibrated threshold on the runner-up plane: five clouds separate cleanly but five clouds cannot place a line that decides whether a camera axis is trustworthy, so that number is published as evidence and gates nothing.

counterexample_the_code_publishes.construction: the Armadillo mesh sampled to 40000 points: no floor, no wall

cost: About 85 ms per plane fit on the 198835-point real scan, so the shipped default of 8 extra fits plus the runner-up costs roughly 0.8 s against a multi-second reconstruction.
reproduce: python docs/evidence/open3d/harness/up_axis_ambiguity.py, with npa/src on PYTHONPATH in an environment holding Open3D. The constructed rooms are seeded; the fit distributions are not reproducible by construction, which is the finding.
